children: The 18% stake at the centre of the Tata battle, and the extraordinary network of families, friends, lawyers and directors around it.
A story of India's leading families who hold the power, and the professionals who have spent decades at their tables.

On September 17, the board of Tata Sons voted to give its chairman N Chandrasekaran five more years and to prepare India's most coveted private company for the stock market. Noel Tata, the chairman of the Tata Trusts, which owns two-thirds of the company, voted NO. The Trusts' other man on the board voted YES. By nightfall the Trusts had declared the whole vote illegal. And almost nobody was talking about the thing that made it all matter: an 18.37% stake in Tata Sons, owned by a family that badly needs the money.

That stake belongs to the Shapoorji Pallonji group, the family that once gave the Tata Sons a chairman in Cyrus Mistry and watched the Tata's throw him out in 2016. With Tata Sons valued at around Rs 12 lakh crore, the Mistry stake is worth roughly Rs 2.2 lakh crore, making it the most priced asset in Indian business.  But it is also a fortune the Shapoor or the Mistry family cannot spend, since it sits locked inside a company with no stock market price and no easy way out. On the other side sit the Tata Trusts, which own about two-thirds of Tata Sons and want it kept private.
Between them sit an RBI decision, a board vote, a chairman's second term, and a question that has been politely avoided at Mumbai dinner tables for years: should Tata Sons list?

This is not a story about a listing. It's about who needs one, who doesn't, and who sits around the table when that decision is made. In Mumbai's corporate jungle, the people in the room are rarely strangers. This is no conspiracy chart, and nobody needs to be accused of pulling a string. The strings are already visible.
THE 18%
Start with the money.
The SP Group's stake is held through Sterling Investment Corporation and Cyrus Investments, and it has been pledged as collateral against loans.

That pledge has a long history. In 2020, the group's main holding company carried about Rs 9,280 crore in external debt, with group-wide debt estimated at over Rs 30,000 crore. That year, Ratan Tata was reported to be looking for a partner to buy out the Mistry stake, and the SP Group said publicly that it was time to separate from the Tatas after more than 70 years.
Even then, the obstacle was clear. One proxy adviser observed that the Tatas were in no hurry while the SP Group badly needed funds.
The separation never happened.

The debt didn't go away. In 2022, Ares SSG and Farallon agreed to lend the group up to Rs 15,000 crore against its Tata Sons shares, at 24% a year, to repay Indian banks. This July, the group completed a Rs 21,500 crore refinancing and told investors it would monetise part of its Tata Sons stake through a listing or share sale within 18 months.
There is the central tension. The SP Group needs liquidity. The Tata Trusts don't want a listing.

The quieter way out was a small sale. The SP Group discussed selling about 2.5% of Tata Sons with Noel Tata, through a tax-efficient structure involving a bank or financial institution. The proceeds would have reached the SP Group over time, and Tata Sons might have avoided a listing altogether. The proposal stalled at Tata Sons and reached the board only after the RBI's directive put listing in focus.

This is where the story turns personal. At the Tata Sons board meeting on September 17, Noel Tata made the Mistrys an offer: Tata Sons would buy back enough of their shares to pay them at least Rs 25,000 crore, in two instalments over eighteen months. The family would get its money. Tata Sons would stay private. The Trusts would keep control.

Noel Tata chairs the Trusts that oppose a listing. He is also married to Cyrus Mistry's sister. His offer was an attempt to satisfy both families at once. The Mistrys had already made up their minds: with the smaller sale delayed, they came out in favour of listing, which would let them cash in on the stake and manage their debts more easily. The board answered Noel the same day, by voting for a listing.
Every connection that follows leads back to that 18%.
THE SALE BEFORE THE SALE
The 18% isn't the first SP asset to need a buyer, and the last big buyer was a familiar name.

In October 2021, a Reliance subsidiary agreed with Shapoorji Pallonji and Company, the Daruvala family and Sterling and Wilson Solar to acquire 40% of the solar company in stages. It was the SP Group's second asset sale in a month to cut debt, after Eureka Forbes went to Advent International for Rs 4,400 crore.
Shapoor Mistry welcomed Reliance into the company.
The same debt that now weighs on the 18% had already put SP assets on the market, and Reliance had already been a buyer.
THE MARRIAGES
Mumbai's business families don't just trade with one another. They marry one another.

Noel Tata's wife, Aloo, is Cyrus Mistry's sister, which makes the chairman of the Tata Trusts a brother-in-law of the family that owns the 18%. It also makes him uncle to Cyrus's sons, Firoz and Zahan, whose side of the family inherited Cyrus's half of the Mistry interest. The man leading the Trusts' resistance to a listing is the uncle of young heirs who stand to benefit from one.
Ajay Piramal's son Anand married Isha Ambani in 2018, making Mukesh Ambani and Ajay Piramal in-laws. That matters here because of where Piramal spent the following years.
And Karan Adani married Paridhi Shroff, daughter of Cyril Shroff, whose law firm is now advising the Tata Trusts on the fight over the 18%'s future.
THE BOARDROOMS

In 2016, Tata announced that Ajay Piramal and Venu Srinivasan had joined the Tata Sons board as non-executive directors. Piramal won a second three-year term in 2019. For years, the father-in-law of Mukesh Ambani's daughter sat on the board that would one day have to decide what to do with the 18%.

Srinivasan, the TVS chairman, sits on both sides of the question. He is a Trusts nominee on the Tata Sons board and a Tata Trusts trustee. Last October, the Sir Dorabji Tata Trust renewed his trusteeship on the way to making him a life trustee. When the listing vote came, he would be the one to break with his own chairman.
THE OLD FRIENDS
Some bonds never show up in a shareholder register, but they still shape who stands where.

When Cyrus Mistry died in a road accident in September 2022, Supriya Sule, Sharad Pawar's daughter, tweeted that her brother Cyrus had died. The Tribune described her as one of the few who stood by him through the boardroom wars, and the first to mourn him.

Then there is Mehli Mistry, Cyrus's first cousin, who became Ratan Tata's confidant and helped care for him in his final years. When Ratan Tata died in October 2024, Mehli was named an executor of his will, alongside lawyer Darius Khambata and Tata's half-sisters, Shireen and Deanna Jejeebhoy.

Khambata, a former Advocate General of Maharashtra, had once mediated between Ratan Tata and Cyrus Mistry, as Businessworld reported. He was reported in July to be likely to step away when his own trusteeship ends in November. But in a letter to the Trusts last year, he recalled a moment that now reads like the opening of a tragedy: after Ratan Tata's death, Mehli Mistry proposed Noel Tata as chairman of the Trusts, and Khambata seconded him.

A year later, Noel Tata, Venu Srinivasan and Vijay Singh opposed Mehli's reappointment, ending his time on the two main Trusts, the ones that control the majority of Tata Sons. The man who proposed Noel was voted off with Noel's vote.
THE RBI TABLE
The same corporate world was represented at the Reserve Bank's central table long before the listing fight reached its present stage.

When S. Gurumurthy joined the RBI board in 2018, N Chandrasekaran was already a member. Gurumurthy is a Chennai-based chartered accountant, editor of the Tamil weekly Thuglak, and widely described as a leading RSS ideologue. Months later, Shaktikanta Das became governor.

Born in Bhubaneswar, Das had spent much of his IAS career in the Tamil Nadu cadre, including a stint as the state's Principal Secretary (Industries). In 2022 the government added Anand Mahindra, Venu Srinivasan, Pankaj Patel and Ravindra Dholakia to the board, bringing another Chennai industrialist, and a Tata Trusts trustee, to the table.

Das left Mint Street in December 2024 and now serves as Principal Secretary-2 to the Prime Minister. The decision that would matter most to Tata Sons came later, under his successor, when the RBI refused to let Tata Sons give up its registration and escape the rule that it must list.
THE LAWYERS
Mumbai's legal village is smaller still.

Cyril Shroff, who has advised most of India's billionaire families from the Ambanis to the Adanis, is personally advising Noel Tata and the Trusts. His team includes Bharat Vasani, Tata Sons' group general counsel for more than 17 years. Senior advocates Aspi Chinoy, Janak Dwarkadas, Abhishek Manu Singhvi and Mukul Rohatgi have reportedly been retained on the same side.

Across the aisle is Shuva Mandal. At Shardul Amarchand Mangaldas, the firm run by Cyril Shroff's brother, he advised Tata Sons when it removed Cyrus Mistry in 2016, and later became the group's general counsel. Earlier, at AZB & Partners, his clients included Reliance. His firm, Anagram Partners, now represents Tata Sons and Chandrasekaran.

Then there's Harish Salve, who has appeared for Reliance over the years and argued for Tata Sons against Cyrus Mistry. He now advises Tata Sons and Chandra, and has argued publicly that Tata Sons should become a public company, the outcome the holders of the 18% now want.

So two brothers run rival firms that have sat on opposite sides of the same boardroom. Two former Tata general counsels advise opposing camps. The Trusts' lawyer is the Adanis' in-law, and Tata Sons' lawyers have Reliance on their CVs.
THE VOTE
On September 17, the Tata Sons board voted 4–1 to reappoint Chandrasekaran as executive chairman for five more years from February 2027, and to take steps towards a listing.

Noel Tata voted against both proposals, while the Trusts' other nominee, Venu Srinivasan, voted in favour. The Trusts' own directors split. The Trusts then declared the vote invalid, arguing that their nominees' affirmative approval was required.

Five days later, Sharad Pawar publicly backed the Trusts, saying their rights and the group's charitable ownership must be protected. The family that mourned Cyrus Mistry as a brother was now defending the Trusts his brother-in-law chairs, while Cyrus's own family backed the listing the Trusts oppose. Pawar's politics is a different story altogether. And he knows well that the incumbent government may want the exact opposite of what he proposes.
THE TIMELINE
Laid end to end, the chronology tells a story of its own.
2016: Cyrus Mistry is removed as Tata Sons chairman. Ajay Piramal and Venu Srinivasan join the Tata Sons board.
2018: Gurumurthy joins the RBI board, where Chandrasekaran already sits. Shaktikanta Das becomes governor. Isha Ambani marries Anand Piramal.
2020: The SP Group says it is time to separate from the Tatas. Ratan Tata is reported to be seeking a buyer for the Mistry stake.
2021: Reliance buys into SP's Sterling and Wilson Solar.
2022: The SP Group borrows against its Tata Sons shares at 24%. Venu Srinivasan joins the RBI board. Cyrus Mistry dies.
October 2024: Ratan Tata dies. Noel Tata becomes Trusts chairman, proposed by Mehli Mistry and seconded by Darius Khambata.
October 2025: Mehli Mistry is voted off the Trusts.
July 2026: The SP Group refinances Rs 21,500 crore and promises to monetise its Tata Sons stake within 18 months.

September 2026: The RBI rejects Tata Sons' deregistration bid. The SP Group backs listing. Noel Tata offers a Rs 25,000 crore buyback. The board reappoints Chandrasekaran 4–1, with Noel against and Venu in favour. The Trusts declare the vote invalid. Sharad Pawar backs the Trusts.
THE CONNECTIONS ARE VISIBLE
Was this simply the machinery of a complicated ownership structure finally colliding with regulation? Or did the people around the table have very different ideas about what should happen to the 18%?

The record doesn't show anyone planning anything, and the connections cut in every direction. The Trusts' own nominees split their vote. The Trusts' chairman offered his in-laws a way out that kept Tata Sons private; they chose the market instead. The Pawars mourned a Mistry and backed the Trusts. The lawyers have worked for everyone.
Follow the 18% and it takes you through half of Mumbai's elite class: its weddings, its boardrooms, its central bank, its courtrooms and its funerals.
The club is small. The stake is large. And the connections have been in plain sight all along. The Tata Club is a story of these Hereditary Businessclass Aristocrats who hold all the power.
Palak Shah

BW Reporters Palak Shah is a seasoned investigative journalist and the fearless author of The Market Mafia: Chronicle of India’s High-Tech Stock Market Scandal & The Cabal That Went Scot-Free, a hard-hitting exposé that unmasked the shadowy underbelly of India’s financial markets. With nearly two decades of boots-on-the-ground reporting in Mumbai, Palak has carved a reputation as a relentless truth-seeker, diving deep into the nexus of money, power, and regulation. His bylines have graced India’s most prestigious financial dailies, including The Economic Times, Business Standard, The Financial Express, and The Hindu Business Line, where his incisive coverage has shaped narratives and rattled boardrooms.

Drawn to crime reporting at the tender age of 19, Palak quickly realized that Mumbai’s gritty gang wars of the 1980s had given way to a slicker, more insidious form of organized crime—white-collar schemes orchestrated in corporate towers. This epiphany fueled his pivot to financial journalism, where he’s spent years decoding the complex machinations of India’s ‘white money’ economy.

From stock market manipulations to regulatory loopholes, Palak’s work peels back the polished veneer of high finance to reveal the cabals pulling the strings. His passion for uncovering truth, backed by a knack for connecting dots others miss, makes him a formidable voice in Indian journalism, unafraid to challenge the status quo and expose the players who think they’re untouchable.
